questionnaire.1.comments: {"comment": "Thanks — the instructions were clear and the task was engaging. I adopted a simple, consistent strategy (keeping 6 tokens each round) to balance private and public payoffs. I noticed the group contributions were fairly stable (around 25 tokens after the first round) and my round earnings varied; the last round’s higher payoff was surprising given the same personal contribution, so I would appreciate clarification on how endowments were assigned each round and how that interacted with the public total. Suggestions: show individual contributions (anonymously) or summary statistics for the group each round, vary the multiplier in some sessions to test sensitivity, and include a brief debrief explaining payoff calculations and an example of final real payout. Overall, it was a well-designed and thought-provoking public-goods task.", "speculation_score": 0.20}

questionnaire.1.comments: {"comment": "Overall the instructions were clear and the payoff structure made the social dilemma easy to understand. With a multiplier of 2.0 split among 4 players, contributing is socially beneficial but privately costly (you get only 0.5 back per token you contribute), which explains moderate contributions and stable behavior across rounds. Anonymity and lack of communication limited reciprocity and punishment, so cooperation stayed at a middling level. Suggestions: (1) consider varying the multiplier or group size to test sensitivity to marginal per-capita return, (2) allow limited communication or reputation information in some conditions to see effects on cooperation, and (3) report individual contributions (or anonymized histories) to study reciprocity dynamics. Overall it was a well-designed, clear experiment that captures the classic public-goods tradeoff.", "speculation_score": 0.10}

questionnaire.1.comments: {"comment": "Overall the experiment is clear and straightforward: instructions, payoff structure, and round feedback are easy to follow. I appreciate the anonymity and the repeated rounds, which let you observe behavior over time. A few suggestions: (1) Consider showing each agent’s individual contribution history (anonymized) or at least giving participants feedback on their own past contributions — that would help participants learn and adjust strategies. (2) Clarify how endowments are randomly assigned each round (is it uniform?) and whether any demographic or behavioral data will be linked to payments. (3) Report how tokens convert to real payment and the timeline for receiving payment. (4) Include comprehension checks so everyone understands the payoff math before starting. (5) If the goal is to study cooperation, consider varying the multiplier or group size across treatments and adding short questionnaires about motives (e.g., beliefs about others’ contributions, fairness preferences). One observation from the feedback: the total public contribution stayed at 11 across rounds while my total earnings varied, which implies my private-kept tokens changed — I would have liked to see my own contribution explicitly in the feedback. questionnaire.1.comments: {"comment": "Overall the instructions and example were clear and the task was straightforward. The design nicely captures the tension between private incentives and collective benefit. Because feedback only showed total group contributions (not individual contributions), it was hard to tell whether low totals reflected a few free-riders or everyone contributing little; providing individual contribution feedback or allowing limited communication could reveal interesting dynamics. I tended to keep my contribution constant across rounds; asking participants to explain their motives after each round would help interpret behavior. It would also be useful to state how tokens convert to real payment up front.
